alalal-e92355-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 4: whether an article constrains to explicit or implicit belief.

alalal-e92355-d1e113.summary: States the fourth question: since an article is named from constraining to belief, does it constrain to explicit or implicit belief?

alalal-e92355-d1e124.summary: First argument for implicit belief: one is not bound to believe what is wholly unknown, and Jerome's gloss on Isaiah 63:1 says some angels did not fully know the mystery of the incarnation until it was accomplished; what angels did not know was not known to humans.

alalal-e92355-d1e161.summary: Second: Ephesians 3:10 says the mystery was made known to the principalities in heaven, so humans were not bound to know it explicitly.

alalal-e92355-d1e172.summary: Third: Chrysostom says we are highly honoured that the angels learned with us through John's voice.

alalal-e92355-d1e186.summary: Fourth: the Gloss on 'gather the fragments' says the fragments are sacred mysteries the common people cannot grasp, so not everyone is bound to believe the articles explicitly.

alalal-e92355-d1e209.summary: Fifth: the Gloss on Ephesians 3:9 says the mystery was hidden from the creatures of all ages, in God's knowledge alone.

alalal-e92355-d1e228.summary: Sixth, by reason: in demonstrative science one can know something universally yet doubt it in a particular, as with the angle-sum of a wooden triangle; much more in faith, which is wholly above reason.

alalal-e92355-d1e254.summary: Seventh: if articles constrained to explicit belief, many who do not know how to distinguish the articles would have been and would be damned.

alalal-e92355-d1e268.summary: Eighth: then things other than articles would also constrain belief, as Hebrews 11:3 on the world framed by God's word.

alalal-e92355-d1e281.summary: Ninth: many things in Hebrews 11, such as Moses hidden three months and Rahab not perishing, are not articles but are received under faith as consequences; so no one is bound to explicit belief.

alalal-e92355-d1e301.summary: Tenth: Lombard says this in the second part of the distinction.

alalal-e92355-d1e308.summary: Sed contra: Boethius says evil is avoided only if known; everyone must avoid unbelief against each article, so each must be known explicitly.

alalal-e92355-d1e324.summary: Second: Galatians 5:3 says whoever is circumcised is bound to the whole law, so whoever receives faith must believe all the articles explicitly.

alalal-e92355-d1e346.summary: Third: if implicit belief in an omnipotent redeemer sufficed, all philosophers and many heretics would have implicit faith, which is false.

alalal-e92355-d1e363.summary: Fourth: in Leviticus 14 the cleansed leper offers a sextarius of oil, which the Gloss calls the measure of faith, neither more nor less; so one must offer the whole measure of articles.

alalal-e92355-d1e381.summary: Fifth: Moses was told to write the law clearly on stones (Deuteronomy 27:8), which the Gloss says are the laity; so they must believe the articles clearly.

alalal-e92355-d1e394.summary: Sixth: faith comes from hearing the word of Christ; hearing makes all explicit and God's word proposes nothing implicitly, so the faithful should believe explicitly.

alalal-e92355-d1e410.summary: Seventh: laymen are arrested and examined on the most hidden articles, and if found erring and ignorant are left as heretics, so they must know and believe explicitly.

alalal-e92355-d1e426.summary: Eighth: suppose a simple, pious old woman hears heresy from her pastor and believes it because she thinks she must believe whatever he says; is she damned if she dies thus, or to be burned as a heretic? It seems not, since ignorance excuses; if so, she must know the articles explicitly even untaught.

alalal-e92355-d1e459.summary: Ninth: charity concerns love of God and neighbour and must know both distinctly, so faith must know the articles distinctly.

alalal-e92355-d1e473.summary: Solution, without prejudice: neither before nor after Christ's coming is anyone bound to know the articles explicitly without divine revelation and teaching, only implicitly; but revelation is certainly made, and always has been, to the Church, and those who receive it are the 'greater', by whom others are instructed. Formerly revelation manifested the articles; now it expounds them, all needing belief having been declared. The simple, before and after, are bound to explicit knowledge only so far as taught by the greater and able to grasp it; those before were bound less, given the shadowy teaching then, those after more, given the open teaching of truth.
claims: The simple are bound to explicit faith only so far as they have been taught and can understand.
Revelation is always given to the Church through the 'greater', who instruct others.
Those after Christ are bound to more explicit faith than those before, because of clearer teaching.

alalal-e92355-d1e525.summary: Reply to Boethius: knowledge is explicit or implicit; one need not know every evil in particular, but avoid it under a wise man's counsel; so in faith, if a new doctrine is proposed, one should turn to the priest and believe or not by his judgment.

alalal-e92355-d1e554.summary: Reply to Galatians: one is bound to the whole faith implicitly, so as to disbelieve none of it.
claims: Implicit faith means disbelieving no article.

alalal-e92355-d1e563.summary: Reply on philosophers and heretics: they did not believe implicitly, since they disbelieved; the implicit believer disbelieves no article, though not knowing it explicitly.

alalal-e92355-d1e581.summary: Reply on the measure: it is filled by disbelieving none, as said.

alalal-e92355-d1e590.summary: Reply on Deuteronomy: it is provided that the faith be often and clearly explained to the laity, which can be done in the time of grace; but because their understanding is dull, they are not bound to understand as explicitly as it is explained, receiving it according to their capacity. Before Christ it could be done only in shadow and type, and they were bound less.
claims: The laity receive explanation according to their capacity and are bound accordingly.

alalal-e92355-d1e622.summary: Reply on hearing: though faith is received distinctly by hearing, the simple understand what they hear only in a folded, indistinct way.

alalal-e92355-d1e635.summary: Reply on examined laity: they are not left as heretics for not knowing how to distinguish articles, but for pertinaciously contradicting them when explained, which could only happen if they had received unbelief from heretics; if ignorance of distinctions were the criterion, the inquisitors themselves would have to be burned, since they do not know them very well either.
claims: Laypeople are judged heretics for pertinacious contradiction, not for ignorance of distinctions.

alalal-e92355-d1e661.summary: Reply on the old woman: the doctors answer doubtfully, but all agree she sins mortally if she disbelieves an article pertinaciously; if she doubts while ready to be corrected, it is human temptation. Some say if she does what she can in works of piety God will enlighten her not to believe the priest; but this rests on uncertainty. Others say: if it concerns an open article celebrated by the Church, she should inquire whether it is commonly held, since faith is common, not one person's; if it concerns something hidden, such as that fornication is no sin or that Christ's body is only signified on the altar, she should accept it only conditionally, if the universal Church believes it, and remain in implicit faith, though the shamefulness of fornication shows her it is mortal sin. This case often arises in confession through priests' lust persuading women.
claims: A simple believer misled by her pastor should hold the Church's common faith and accept novel teaching only conditionally on the Church's belief.
Pertinacious disbelief of an article is always mortal sin.

alalal-e92355-d1e737.summary: Reply to the last: charity is not similar, since it seeks only its object, not reasons, and does not distinguish, loving the neighbour only materially; faith is mixed with cognition and understanding, for which not all are sufficient.

alalal-e92355.summary: Article 4 asks whether the articles bind to explicit or only implicit belief. Arguments for implicit belief cite angelic ignorance of the incarnation, mysteries hidden from the people, and the many simple believers. Arguments for explicit belief cite the need to know evils to avoid them, the whole measure of faith, the examination of laymen, and the case of a pious old woman misled by her pastor into heresy. Albert holds, without prejudice, that without revelation and teaching no one is bound to explicit faith. Revelation is always given to the Church through the 'greater', who instruct the rest: formerly it manifested the articles, now it expounds them. The simple are bound to explicit faith only so far as they have been taught and can grasp it, those after Christ more than those before. Implicit faith means disbelieving no article, which separates it from philosophers and heretics. Laypeople are judged heretics for pertinacity, not ignorance, and otherwise the inquisitors themselves would be condemned. A believer misled by a priest should hold the Church's common faith and accept novel teaching only conditionally; Albert notes that such cases often arise from priests' abuse in confession.
claims: The simple are bound to explicit faith only so far as they have been taught and can understand.
Implicit faith means disbelieving no article, which distinguishes it from the unbelief of philosophers and heretics.
Heresy consists in pertinacious contradiction, not ignorance.
Believers should hold the common faith of the Church and accept novel teachings only conditionally.
